title: Dishes You Can Cook From the Pantry
statement:
A cooking app knows n dishes. Dish recipes[i] needs every item in ingredients[i]. An ingredient can be a basic item or another dish from the list, which you would have to cook first.

Your pantry has an unlimited amount of every item in supplies. Once you cook a dish, you can use it as an ingredient as many times as you like.

Return every dish you can end up cooking, in any order.

examples.why: Toast needs only pantry items. Sandwich needs toast, which you can cook first.
Each dish waits on the other, so neither can ever be cooked. A dependency cycle blocks every dish on it.
Onion is neither in the pantry nor a dish you can cook, so soup is impossible. Salad does not depend on it.

constraints: Names are 1 to 10 lowercase letters or digits
Dish names are distinct and never appear in supplies
A dish never lists itself or the same ingredient twice
hints: Think of each dish as a node that becomes available once all its ingredients are available. Which dishes can you cook right away?
Cooking a dish might unlock others that were waiting on it. For every dish, keep a count of how many of its ingredients you do not have yet.

Topological order (Kahn's algorithm): put every pantry item in a queue. When you take an item off, decrease the missing-count of every dish that needs it; a dish whose count hits 0 is cookable and goes into the queue too. Dishes on a cycle or behind a missing item never reach 0.

explain.intuition:
This is a dependency graph, like a build tool deciding which packages can be built. Draw an edge from each ingredient to each dish that needs it. A dish is cookable when everything pointing into it is available: a pantry item or an already cooked dish.

Kahn's algorithm processes exactly that. Each dish keeps a counter of ingredients still missing. Start a queue with all pantry items. Taking an item off the queue satisfies one ingredient of each dish that uses it; when a dish's counter reaches 0, it is cooked and joins the queue as a new available item. Dishes stuck on a cycle or on an item nobody has never reach 0, so they are left out automatically.
steps: For each dish i, set missing[i] = ingredients[i].length and add i to users[ing] for each of its ingredients.
Put every supply into a queue.
Pop an item. For each dish i in users[item], decrease missing[i].
When missing[i] reaches 0, add recipes[i] to the answer and push it into the queue.
When the queue is empty, return the answer.
pitfalls: Checking each dish only once in input order. A dish can depend on one listed after it, so a single pass misses it.
Recursing into dependencies without cycle detection, which loops forever on the second example.
Treating an ingredient that is neither a supply nor a dish as available.

solutions.title: Repeat passes until nothing changes
solutions.idea: Keep a set of available items. Sweep all dishes; cook any whose ingredients are all available. Stop when a sweep cooks nothing.

solutions.title: Topological order with missing-ingredient counts
solutions.idea: Kahn's algorithm: start from the pantry; each available item lowers the missing count of the dishes that use it, and a dish at zero becomes available itself.

followups: Return the dishes in an order you could actually cook them.
Each pantry item now has a limited quantity and each dish consumes one of each ingredient. Why does the problem get much harder?
